read: full (all 7 pages: abstract, introduction, related work, dataset composition and construction, evaluation protocol, experiments, conclusion, references)
venue_now: arXiv preprint 2507.04766v1, 7 Jul 2025 (p. 1 header); the text shows no venue
what_it_is: A physics benchmark of 500 problems that all require a precise numerical answer (p. 1, p. 3). Phy_A holds 400 fixed graduate- or Olympiad-level problems, selected by an 'experimental screening' for cases where models give long, low-accuracy answers (p. 3); Phy_B holds 100 problems whose numerical constants, embedded in the ground-truth LaTeX solutions, are perturbed by a variation engine to produce variants with the same physical model, and a Phy_B problem counts as solved only if every variant is answered correctly (p. 2, p. 3, p. 4). Items come from textbooks and examination papers, OCR'd, manually annotated, rewritten by DeepSeek-R1 under human review, paraphrased by an independent reviewer and verified by one to two annotators (p. 3). Answers are scored automatically at a 1% relative tolerance (p. 4); 15 LLMs are evaluated, the best scoring 43.0% on Phy_A, and accuracy falls by 22.5 points on average from the static to the perturbed Phy_B versions (p. 2, p. 4).
domain: physics, advanced undergraduate to graduate and Olympiad level: classical mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum physics, electrodynamics, semiconductor and fluid mechanics, atomic physics and other modern topics (p. 3)
size: 500 problems: 400 static (Phy_A) and 100 parameterised (Phy_B), released with three variations per Phy_B problem (p. 3, Table 1 and footnote 2); 15 models in Table 2 (p. 4)
source_of_items: textbooks and examination papers, digitised by OCR, manually extracted and annotated, scenario rewrites by DeepSeek-R1 reviewed by humans, paraphrased by an independent reviewer (p. 3); Phy_A screened for difficulty against models (p. 3); Phy_B variants generated by numeric perturbation (p. 2-3)
instances: static (Phy_A, 400) and perturbed (Phy_B, 100 problems whose numeric constants are regenerated; three variants each in the preprint release, p. 3 footnote 2; the engine is 'still ongoing')
has_gold_traces: partial: each problem has a verified reference solution in LaTeX ('every question - along with its corresponding solution - was independently verified', p. 3; Phy_B variants are generated from 'the ground-truth LaTeX solutions', p. 3), but the paper does not say the solutions are released for evaluation, and scoring never uses them (p. 4)
evaluation: final answer only: a LaTeX-based parser extracts a number, accepted when |y_hat - y*| <= 0.01 |y*| (relative error at most 1%); each question states the required unit and number of significant figures; a Phy_B problem is credited only if all its regenerated variants are correct (p. 2, p. 4)
human_validation: Every question and solution was independently verified by one to two annotators who solved it step by step; DeepSeek-R1 rewrites were manually reviewed and refined; symbolic derivations and numeric endpoints were 'independently produced and cross-verified' (p. 3). No inter-annotator agreement, error rate or validation of the answer checker is reported.
contamination_measures: perturbations (Phy_B numeric-constant variants, p. 2-3); paraphrasing of each question by an independent reviewer 'to minimize overlap with publicly available pre-training corpora' and scenario rewrites by DeepSeek-R1 (p. 3). No private test set or recency cut-off is described.

engtrace_use.sentence: S-P1 (L172-177): 'While UGPhysics (Xu et al., 2025) and PhysReason (Zhang et al., 2025a) effectively test the application of reasoning to natural laws, others target advanced symbolic (Zhang et al., 2025b; Qiu et al., 2025) or qualitative (Wang et al., 2023; Shojaee et al., 2025) understanding.' S-P2 (L177-180): 'Despite this progress, these benchmarks remain confined to theoretical physics, lacking the integrative context of engineering.' R-1 (July 2026 rebuttal, not in the paper): 'ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) uses a 1% tolerance for physics reasoning.'
engtrace_use.explanation: 'Advanced' fits: Phy_A is graduate- or Olympiad-level (p. 1, p. 3). 'Symbolic' does not: the benchmark 'focuses exclusively on numerical calculation problems' (p. 2, p. 5) and defines itself against benchmarks that 'required answers in the form of expressions (Qiu et al., 2025b), which are difficult to evaluate precisely' (p. 2), so grouping it with PHYBench under 'symbolic' inverts its own positioning. More important for EngTrace, the sentence omits Phy_B, a parameterised subset whose numeric constants are perturbed to generate variants and which credits a problem only if all variants are solved (p. 2-4): the closest physics precedent for EngTrace's generated, contamination-resistant instances, and a direct qualification of the Introduction's suggestion that parameterisation sets EngTrace apart (S-I3). S-P2 is loose for this paper: its content is textbook and exam physics (mechanics, electromagnetism, optics, quantum, semiconductor and fluid mechanics, p. 3), not theoretical physics, although it has no engineering context. R-1 is accurate: an answer is accepted when its relative error does not exceed 1% (p. 4; 'a strict 1% tolerance for error', p. 2).

suggested_wording: ABench-Physics (Zhang et al., 2025b) pairs 400 fixed graduate- and Olympiad-level problems with 100 problems whose numerical constants are perturbed to generate variants, accepting an answer within a 1% relative tolerance and crediting a perturbed problem only if every variant is solved; accuracy falls by 22.5 points on average from the static to the perturbed versions, though only final answers are scored.
facts_to_cite: 500 problems in two parts: Phy_A, 400 static graduate- or Olympiad-level problems, and Phy_B, 100 problems with an automatic variation engine (p. 1; Table 1, p. 3).

Problems were collected from textbooks and examination papers, digitised by OCR, manually annotated, rewritten by DeepSeek-R1 with human review, paraphrased by an independent reviewer to reduce overlap with pre-training corpora, and each verified by one to two annotators who solved it (p. 3).
Phy_A problems were chosen by 'experimental screening' for cases where models give long responses with low accuracy (p. 3).

Phy_B regenerates variants by perturbing the numerical constants in the ground-truth LaTeX solutions, keeping the physical model fixed (p. 2, p. 3); the preprint release has three variations per Phy_B problem and the engine is described as still in development (p. 3, footnote 2).
All answers are numerical; each question specifies its unit and number of significant figures; an answer is correct when its relative error is at most 1% (p. 2, p. 4).
A Phy_B problem is credited only if all its variants are answered correctly (p. 2, p. 4).
The best model (Gemini 2.5 Pro with reasoning) scores 43.0% on Phy_A (p. 2; Table 2, p. 4).

Accuracy drops by 22.5% on average from static to dynamic Phy_B versions, nearly 28% for the most affected model (p. 2, p. 4); Table 2's Delta column shows these are absolute drops in accuracy (mean 0.225 over the 15 models, my arithmetic).
Only the final numerical answer is scored (p. 4); the benchmark deliberately excludes expression answers (p. 2, p. 5).
overlap_with_engtrace: Shares: free-response numerical answers graded within a relative tolerance (1% here; EngTrace's answer check uses REL 0.002, state brief section 2) with the unit and significant figures specified; a parameterised subset whose numeric constants are regenerated, credited only if every variant is solved, which is the nearest physics analogue to EngTrace's template-generated instances; human-verified reference solutions. Lacks: generation beyond numeric perturbation of 100 problems (three variants each in the release; the 400 Phy_A problems are fixed); gold traces used in evaluation; any step-level or process evaluation (final answer only, p. 4); an engineering setting (physics only; fluid mechanics and semiconductors appear as physics topics, p. 3); validation of the evaluator against experts; a private pool or hash commitment. Positioning caution: 54 to 58 of EngTrace's 150 templates follow one reasoning path in all 15 instances (state brief section 1), so the revised text should not present numeric-variant generation as new relative to ABench-Physics; EngTrace's difference lies in gold traces with step-level verification, the engineering scope and expert validation of the evaluator.
notes: The May reference list misprints all 12 given names of this entry (citation_context_map.md). Internal slip in the paper: p. 4 says Table 2 presents 'four widely used large language models' while the table lists 15. The paper writes the static-to-dynamic decline as '22.5%'; it is an absolute accuracy drop (0.225), not a relative one. ABench-Physics and PHYBench sit on opposite sides of a numeric-versus-symbolic answer split, and ABench-Physics draws that contrast itself (p. 2), so the revised paragraph should not group them as 'symbolic'. For this paper alone, 'scores only the final answer' would be an accurate characterisation.
